sports.description: PALM BEACH GARDENS, Fla. — Atlanta Drive's Charley Hull stood in a bunker at SoFi Center holding a conversation with team owner Arthur Blank. Hull, whose team would make its WTGL debut about 30 minutes later, then grabbed her wedge, and as Blank was walking away, holed a 30-footer. Looking on and nodding with approval was Billy Horschel, a star on Atlanta's TGL team. For Hull — and Atlanta — that proved to be the highlight of the night. Even with Horschel and Justin Thomas, both part of Atlanta's championship winning team in TGL's inaugural season, lending support from the team owner's box, Boston Common Golf defeated Atlanta, 8-3, Tuesday at SoFi Center. Boston Common had the advantage of playing its second WTGL match. "Obviously it wasn't the result that we wanted, but we had a great laugh," Hull said in perhaps the most upbeat post-game press conference ever held by a losing team. "It is a lot of fun. It's nice actually to be ... I know we're not on the golf course, but you're in the golf environment, and having a laugh." Hull, one of the marquee names playing in WTGL's first season, is considered the most popular active women's golfer in Europe. The Englishwoman is No. 7 in the world, a three-time winner on the LPGA Tour and although she still is chasing her first major championship, she has five runner-ups in the tour's marquee events. She has played in eight Solheim Cups. Hull, 30, also this year checked off what she called a childhood dream, appearing in the Sports Illustrated Swimsuit edition. All of which makes her a natural for a league that encourages the golfers to let loose and show their personality. Her 869,000 Instagram followers are more than any other golfer on WTGL's 25-woman roster. "I think it's cool that here in WTGL we can expose people that it's actually fun to play golf and dress pretty cool," said Hull's teammate, Nataliya Guseva. "I think that's kind of our goal as well with Charley out here with the Malbon (golf fashion) stuff." Every woman who has played in the league's first four matches agrees the league is part entertainment and fashion along with the competition. Guseva, the 23-year-old Russian, had a rough night, drawing three penalties. She admitted to having nerves and said ... well, here is what she said. "It was super cool, but it was just kind of weird ... to show how nervous I am," she said. sports.description: This has been a challenging season for Penn State’s offense to say the least. Instead of a consistently productive unit that improved as the season went along, they’ve presented a disjointed operation that excels one week and is left searching for answers the next week. The ebbs and flows of the season have been aggressive, even in individual games. A staple of the Nittany Lions offense has been jumping out to double-digit leads in the first half, and then completely falling apart in the second half, whether it be from turnovers or just a lack of execution. Maryland doesn’t have a great defense, but Penn State recently showed that even the worst defenses — like the Rutgers Scarlet Knights — can have success against it. The offense for the blue and white could score 40 points this week, or they could barely hit 20 points and be in a dog fight late in the fourth quarter. It’s impossible to know which version of the Nittany Lions will show up from week to week, but here are the raw numbers about the unit compared to the Terrapins defense. Turnovers Penn State offense: 9 turnovers Maryland defense: 15 takeaways Turnovers have the biggest indicator of whether Penn State will win this season. The team is 6-0 when it doesn’t turn the ball over, and 5-0 when it turns the ball over at all. The Nittany Lions have been one of the best teams in terms of taking care of the ball, currently tied for 18th in the nation with just nine giveaways. However, Maryland ranks in the top-third of college football with 15 takeaways. Linebacker Daniel Wingate has accounted for 20% of those all by himself, so Penn State needs to put an extreme focus on holding onto the ball this week. Passing yards per game Penn State offense: 232.5 Maryland defense: 216.4 Penn State’s passing game hasn’t been without its struggles this season, but it also has been the most reliable means of moving the ball. The air attack is above average nationally, currently ranking 59th out of all FBS teams with 232.5 yards per game. Maryland’s defense is middle of the pack in this category, ranking 75th with 216.4 yards allowed per game. That is the range the defense falls in for most categories. This means that the Terrapins aren’t great on that side of the ball, but they also aren’t a pushover. Rocco Becht will have to be on his A-game on Saturday because one slip up will likely be the game. He has to play a clean game and air the ball out efficiently against Maryland like many other quarterbacks have this year. Follow Nittany Lions Wire on X and Facebook . sports.description: Free agent utilityman Mauricio Dubon The Baltimore Orioles signed Freddy Peralta to a five-year, $125 million deal, but they may not be done adding to their team. The Orioles could use some help on offense, and according to The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal and Will Sammon , they are showing interest in Mauricio Dubón, among other players. Dubón is an interesting target for any team. He is a versatile defender who can play all over the field and is coming off a career year with the bat. The big question, however, is whether he can continue being a force at the plate. He set career highs in hits, RBIs, extra-base hits, walks and on-base percentage. He won his third career Gold Glove Award. He has had one other season where he was this good offensively, and it came in 2023 with the Houston Astros. The Orioles could use Dubón in the outfield, or as an option at second base if Jackson Holliday cannot figure things out. Regardless, players in Dubón's tier of free agents are where the Orioles should be expected to shop. He is 32 years old and may not get a long-term deal. However, there is a real possibility that Castillo could find a way to rebound after the worst season of his career and be a monumental pickup for the Rockies. sports.description: Henry Cejudo and Eddie Cha celebrate win at UFC 249. | UFC Eddie Cha, one of the sport’s top striking coaches, has suddenly died. Multiple people with knowledge of the situation confirmed to MMA Fighting that Cha passed away at the age of 53. The cause of death is unknown at this time. Cha worked with the likes of Henry Cejudo, Chan Sung Jung, Tracy Cortez, Zhang Weili, Kelvin Gastelum, and many other notable names in the sport of mixed martial arts. Cejudo, who Cha helped coach to UFC world championship gold, reacted to the news on Instagram days before getting ready to face Song Yadong at RAF 15. technology.title: Microsoft fixes Office dialog that had nothing to say and wouldn't go away
technology.description: Microsoft has released a fix for a baffling bug that threw a blank window over Office applications and brought work to a standstill. The problem appeared when users launched an affected Office app, which could display an empty dialog box with no text and no buttons. Because the dialog offered no way to close it, some users were locked out of their work entirely, unable to continue until the issue was resolved. The good news is that there's an update to fix the problem – version 2611, build 16.0.20625.20142. The bad news is that you might not be able to launch the applications to perform the update because of that blank dialog window. Microsoft instructs affected users to save their work, close all Office applications, and open Command Prompt as administrator. They can then force the update with: "%programfiles%\Common Files\Microsoft Shared\ClickToRun\officec2rclient.exe" /update user updatetoversion=16.0.20625.20142 The glitch affects a swathe of Microsoft 365 products – Excel, Word, Outlook, PowerPoint, Access, and OneNote. Users reported the problem on Microsoft's forums , where volunteer moderator Stefan Blom noted that "this seems to be a common error at the moment" and suggested users try an Office repair or the more thorough Online Repair. Online Repair reinstalls Office, however, some users reported activation and sign-in problems alongside the blank windows, which may hint at the cause. Microsoft has yet to elucidate. Other users found that rolling back Office resolved the issue, while several reported that signing in with another application, such as Edge, fixed things. For administrators preparing fleets of devices, a dialog that blocks first use creates another deployment headache. One user with E3 licensing reported: "We can't just hand off a staged machine without getting call[s] that our new users can't get Office to work because of the blank licensing window." Microsoft has shared a fix for the problem, but has not stated which versions of its productivity applications were affected, nor has it explained what went wrong. The fix is welcome. An explanation of how Office ended up blocking users with a window containing nothing at all would be welcome too. ®

technology.title: JetBrains finds agents may cheat with open source
technology.description: JetBrains has revamped a benchmark for evaluating large language models after suspecting too many agents gamed their tasks the first time round. The company labelled this agentic practice "reward hacking" in a post summarizing the results of its revised evaluation. Like its predecessor , Kotlin Benchmark 2.0 is a collection of tasks that evaluates how well AI coding agents work with the Kotlin programming language , in order to help Kotlin programmers decide which agent-model configurations to use. The tasks include fixing tricky problems in Kotlin code across different domains, and making corrections to multiple files. Dirty data The revised benchmar k now includes 30 Kotlin multi-file code problems that have not been exposed to the public in any way before. The revised test all but guarantees that the agents have not encountered this set of problems, or potential solutions, before. Another 70 tasks are based on code that resides in public repositories. The test also blocked all network access for the open source tasks, except for what was needed to communicate with the model itself. This minimized the possibility that the agent could look for an existing answer already posted, perhaps through a patch or pull request. A 30-minute limit was set for each task. Overall, the agents were significantly less accurate when solving problems on codebases they had never encountered. Top resolution rates dropped rather suspiciously from 86.2 percent on tasks based on open source repositories to 60 percent on those based on closed source repositories. Although the agents lacked network access, JetBrains boffins theorized that they might have benefited from encountering and internalizing these open source repositories during training. Only the private repositories were completely new to them. Also curious was how a different set of models excelled at the closed source problems, compared to those models that usually did better on the open source tasks. Of the two, the open weight DeepSeek was far cheaper (at $0.08 per task) than the closed weight Gemini ($1.74 per task), however. In contrast, Opus 5.5 completed only 53.3 percent of the tasks at $1.21 per task, and Fable 5.1 completed only 44.4 percent of the tasks, at a luxurious $3.27 per task. Claude Code harnessed both of these models. technology.description: Win4Wine is one of the more remarkable and creative hacks we've read about in recent years. It runs Windows XP's genuine Explorer shell through patched Wine on Debian 13, with a custom window manager integrating Linux applications into the desktop. As its GitHub repository explains: "The taskbar, Start menu, desktop and folder windows are XP's real ones, and Linux applications get XP's frames and taskbar buttons." This impressive, possibly demented project has English installation instructions and a README, although its design documents are in Japanese. We found Mozilla's built-in translation handled those pretty well. Its developer goes by miKuta0407 on GitHub, their homepage , and X . Also note, you're going to need some Windows installation media for the full experience. The README says: "No Microsoft files are included. Only the files that are needed are extracted locally from your own ISO." Without either Windows image, it can download and use ReactOS's free software shell instead, for what it terms "a Windows 2000-like classic look." In our view, that sounds much better anyway. The top of the README warns: "This is a personal, experimental project, not a finished product for daily use." The developer has tested it only on a fresh Debian 13 installation and recommends a VM or spare machine, rather than an existing working desktop, which sounds like an excellent precaution to us. Also, before you ask, yes, it was vibe-coded with Claude. technology.title: Microsoft 365 Backup stretches recovery window to ten years
technology.description: Recovery windows of up to ten years are now available in Microsoft 365 Backup for OneDrive and SharePoint, up from a previous maximum of two. The change took effect on October 31, though Exchange remains capped at two years. Administrators can select recovery windows of three months, six months, or any whole number of years from one to ten. Microsoft's list price is $0.15 per GiB per month of protected content. Extended windows can increase costs by keeping deleted data billable for longer. Switching to a longer recovery window will also not make backups for that period magically available. So no nostalgic trips back to 2016. Wider recovery windows may appeal to organizations that need access to older data, but backups are not a substitute for compliance retention and archiving. Recovery after a breach or ransomware attack is also critical, particularly getting back to a healthy state before any malware seeped into files. Microsoft says backups are physically redundant and geographically replicated while respecting the tenant's data residency requirements. Full OneDrive account and SharePoint site restores offer recovery points every ten minutes for the most recent two weeks, then weekly points through the configured window, up to ten years. Individual file and folder recovery is limited to recovery points from the most recent 14 days, regardless of the configured window. Restore remains free, which is handy since regular testing is a vital part of any disaster recovery plan. The arrival of a ten-year recovery window is good for enterprises that need it and have deep enough pockets. However, it is important to keep in mind that being able to configure a longer recovery window doesn't constitute a disaster recovery plan in itself and may be overkill in many instances. Microsoft notes: "The existing one-year default recovery window remains unchanged. Longer recovery windows must be configured on the applicable backup policies." The company also recommends that users "review your organization's SharePoint and OneDrive backup requirements to determine whether longer recovery windows are needed." A decade of recovery history could be valuable. It also means a decade of data to account for when setting budgets, access controls, and retention policies. ®

In the US, the service now covers more than 150 cities and offers vehicles from 35 brands. Hyundai is the first announced UK carmaker partner, while dealer group Vertu Motors will list used vehicles. Of course, buying a car isn't quite like adding an air fryer or a memory stick to your basket. How does financing and checkout work for UK buyers? Customers will complete the purchase and paperwork at their chosen dealership. Amazon is not offering financing itself, but buyers can explore financing options via the site, adjusting terms like deposit and duration to see how monthly payments change. Credit applications must be completed with the dealer. In the US, buyers can submit a credit application through the platform, review terms and conditions, then sign electronic contracts online. Buyers shouldn't expect their new car to arrive in an enormous cardboard box with a smiley logo on it, or to be lowered onto their driveway by a giant Amazon delivery drone. technology.title: AI may soon change what it means to be a theoretical physicist
technology.description: About six months ago, Suvrat Raju, a professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, India, asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem. He didn’t ask because he needed to know the answer. He had actually solved this particular problem already. But he had never published the solution—which made it a perfect question to test how good AI was at physics. LLMs have been trained on the whole Internet, so if a physics problem has been discussed online, it’s likely the model already knows about it and may have memorized the answer. So a fair test of AI capabilities needs to focus on problems that have never appeared online. The model didn’t answer Raju’s problem correctly, but it did better than he expected—well, enough to get him thinking that the experiment should be repeated and formalized. technology.title: The world's fastest computers have a problem: Keeping the work running
technology.description: Frontier, Oak Ridge National Laboratory's exascale supercomputer, has thousands of processors working together on scientific problems. It also has a surprisingly ordinary way of ruining a researcher's day: one node going down. An uncorrectable memory error can do it, or a maintenance mishap. Scott Atchley , chief technology officer at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, describes technicians accidentally rebooting the wrong node or risking a neighboring node's power supply while working in tightly packed racks. The hardware fault can affect just one node, but a simulation running across thousands of processors can grind to a halt. Then comes a series of questions. How recently did the application save its progress? How much computation needs repeating? And how long before the scheduler lets the job run again? For operators, the challenge isn't just keeping the supercomputer running. It's keeping the science moving. One bad node and everybody suffers On Frontier , a memory error can have an outsized audience. Atchley says uncorrectable double-bit errors in high-bandwidth memory occurred about 1.5 times a day during the supercomputer's early bring-up. Its predecessor, Summit, saw roughly one every two weeks. This sounds like a backward step, until you count the memory. Frontier has more than 16 times as much, giving bad bits considerably more places to hide. Memory isn't the only problem. Problematic GPU firmware can crash a node, and so can a technician rebooting the wrong one. Interconnect faults add another way for a large job to come unstuck. In a tightly coupled simulation using the Message Passing Interface (MPI) simulation, thousands of processes, or ranks, exchange data and participate in collective operations. If one rank disappears, the others cannot carry on as though nothing happened. Clockwork.io CEO Suresh Vasudevan describes a similar dependency in synchronized GPU training. One failed GPU can bring a 1,024-GPU job to a pause. An underperforming GPU can be almost as troublesome: if one participant runs at 80 percent speed, others might have to spend time waiting for it. The bigger the machine, the more ways there are for one small problem to become everybody's problem. How often should you hit save? Since stopping every component from failing isn't an option, researchers need a way to preserve their work. That's where checkpointing comes in. The application periodically saves its state so that, when something goes wrong, the simulation can resume from an earlier point instead of starting from scratch. The catch is that saving progress costs computing time, and doing it too often can become almost as wasteful as losing the work itself. Vasudevan explains this with an example. VMware’s FAQ for the new advisory includes the following remarks: Because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing this VMSA comes on the heels of VMSA-2026-0009, and atop a major holiday in the United States. The security vulnerability landscape is more dynamic than ever; please know that while we acknowledge this timing is not optimal, your ability to operate and maintain a secure environment amidst modern, AI-assisted threats is paramount to us. Make of that what you will as you ponder how and when to patch the four critical flaws, including the 9.8-rated CVE-2026-123903, which allows a malicious actor to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to vCenter, the management tool VMware users rely on to manage hosts and VMs. This is the third 9.8-rated authentication issue VMware has fixed in vCenter since July. Two of the other critical flaws in this new advisory allow an attacker to run code on an ESX host, earning the bugs a 9.8 rating. CVE-2026-123910 makes that possible thanks to a heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the I/O filter service, while CVE-2026-123911 is a use-after-free vulnerability. The other critical flaw, CVE-2026-123912, can result in a guest escape from VMware’s desktop Workstation and Fusion desktop hypervisors. It’s also present in VMware’s ESX hypervisor, but attackers thankfully can’t escape that product’s sandbox. This one’s easy to mitigate because the problem is in a USB controller that users can turn off. Most of the other flaws require installation of updated software. There’s a little good news in that some of the software updates VMware issued last week include fixes for the newly disclosed flaws. But there are still plenty of fresh fixes to apply, across ten products: ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, VMware tools, Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, the Telco Cloud Platform, Telco Cloud Infrastructure, and the VMware Avi Load Balancer. VMware’s advisory thanks external researchers for finding and reporting most of the flaws. The Broadcom business unit is known to be a member of Project Glasswing, the Anthropic-run effort to use the Mythos model to find flaws that has seen many vendors dramatically increase the number of patches they produce. In past years, VMware has often published considerably more than this year’s 11 security advisories. With five weeks left in the year, perhaps vAdmins need to worry Christmas might also get complicated. ®

technology.title: Nutanix CEO announces gradual departure, intent to complete set of storage links
technology.description: Nutanix CEO Rajiv Ramaswami has decided to step down from the job once the company’s board can find his successor. Ramaswami announced his decision on Tuesday and in conversation with The Register said he doesn’t have another job lined up, isn’t sure what he will do next, fancies sitting on boards or advising startups, but will take a break after Nutanix finds its next leader. The CEO moved from VMware to Nutanix in 2020 and characterized his time at the company as writing its “second chapter.” The first, he explained, saw Nutanix focus on hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) and a limited group of workloads, especially desktop virtualization, while struggling to make a profit. In chapter two, Nutanix redefined HCI as “hybrid cloud infrastructure” by enabling its stack to run on-prem or in public clouds, and by adding support for containers alongside VMs. Ramaswami took credit for stabilizing Nutanix’s finances while leading the expansion of its platform and for keeping net promoter scores high while the company grew. The CEO added that Nutanix’s decision to end its devotion to virtualized storage and start to support external arrays was also part of chapter two. Ramaswami said he hopes to expand the number of storage vendors Nutanix supports beyond Dell, Everpure, and NetApp, until it works with all major array suppliers. Chapter 3, he said, will be making Nutanix an AI platform, “by catering to a whole new set of ecosystems.” Ramaswami told The Register he had been thinking about moving on for some time and raised it with the board in recent weeks. In the letter he wrote to Nutanix staff , the CEO said the company's board has begun the search for a successor and said he will remain at his post until a replacement is found and then “continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time.” News of the CEO’s planned departure came on the same day Nutanix announced its Q1 results, which saw 15 percent revenue growth to $772.4 million. The company added 410 customers in the quarter, the slowest growth for several years. Ramaswami said high hardware costs remain “a headwind” for Nutanix, but said the company continues to win customers seeking an alternative to VMware. He also pointed to the largest new customer win for the quarter coming from a financial services outfit that uses Dell external storage, a significant score because two years ago Nutanix could not have competed for that business. Nutanix forecast slightly faster growth for the rest of its financial year, suggesting it is not ready to ride AI’s rocket to riches. Investors knocked about ten percent off the company’s share price in after-hours trading, sending it to around $50, roughly double what it was when Ramaswami took over as CEO, but below $79-plus peaks in late 2025. ®

technology.title: Dell and HPE both say they’ve become ‘different companies’
technology.description: Dell and HPE this week both told investors they’ve become “different companies.” The two hardware giants made that assertion on their respective earnings calls this week. HPE went first, on Monday, when CEO Antonio Neri declared “We are now a fundamentally different company” after acquiring Juniper Networks and creating products “built to capitalize on the next phase of AI.” On Tuesday, Dell’s chief operating officer and vice chairman Jeff Clarke declared “We are now a different company” because the Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) has become the source of “the vast majority of our profit and growth.” HPE’s claim to having changed is perhaps more credible on the face of it, given that its acquisition of Juniper means it has become more of a networking player. Dell hasn’t made significant additions to its hardware portfolio, but there’s a big difference in its sources of revenue, which three years ago was just about evenly split between its infrastructure and client devices. In its Tuesday announcement, Dell revealed ISG revenue grew 198 percent year over year to $42 billion, while CSG racked up three percent growth to $12.9 billion – meaning Dell is now predominantly an infrastructure company. Clarke said he’s seen some companies deferring their PC purchases to buy AI hardware instead, and said Dell is re-assigning parts it ordered to build PCs and using them for servers instead. Dell exited its Q3 with a backlog of $32 billion worth of AI servers and is clearly aware that investors might worry that’s not a useful metric because some buyers’ dreams of operating neoclouds have struck financial or regulatory barriers. Clarke assured investors that Dell is “highly selective about the partners we work with” “Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance, and access to land and power.” HPE also has wrinkles in its AI business, because buyers won’t stand for fat margins and that’s dented the company’s profits a little. Neri was able to point to AI-related revenue also rising sharply, up 68.6 percent year over year to $11.3 billion, while overall revenue climbed 50 percent to reach $14.5 billion. Networking grew at a more relaxed 12 percent. The CEO said HPE expects better growth ahead, because new server purchases create demand for networks and storage. He also pointed to HPE having the opportunity to sell its networking kit to other OEMs who build AMD’s Helios rack-scale systems. HPE predicted its next quarter will see revenue reach $14.0 billion to $14.6 billion, up 51 to 57 percent year over year. Dell is also optimistic that AI buyers will spend on kit beyond servers and GPUs and updated its full-year revenue outlook to $202 billion, $10 billion above its previous forecasts and up 78 percent year over year. ®

science.title: Satellites watch volcanic eruptions add new beaches on Iwo Jima | Space photo of the day for Nov. 25, 2026
science.description: null Iwo Jima on Oct. 26, 2026 on the left and the same location on Nov. 11, 2026 shows the impact of a volcanic eruption. (Image credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey ) Iwo Jima looks remarkably different from space after a volcanic eruption created new land extending the Japanese island's beaches. What is it? On Oct. 27, Japan's Meteorological Agency detected an underwater volcanic eruption off the shores of Iwo Jima. Soon after this initial detection of the "submarine" volcano, satellites orbiting our planet started taking a look, observing to see what havoc this eruption might wreak. When you compare the satellite images above captured by the Landsat 9 satellite's Operational Land Imager (OLI), you can see the stark differences between the island on October 26 before the eruption and weeks later on November 11. The island was also observed by NASA's NISAR spacecraft as well as the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) and VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) sensors. Together, this imagery gave researchers a more complete picture of how the eruption continued and the effects it left behind. And amazingly, with satellite imagery experts have been able to show that the eruption has actually added more land to the island's beaches. Why is it incredible? On Nov. 16, Japan's Coast Guard confirmed in a statement that about 125 acres (50 hectares) of new land is now connected to the island's southeast beach following the recent volcanic eruption. This is not the first time that a volcano has created new land. Lava and ash from a volcanic eruption can solidify and accumulate, adding land material around the volcano or to a nearby coast if it is located offshore or underwater, as we saw in this case. But these new landforms aren't always permanent fixtures. This new addition to the island's beach could easily and quickly be washed away by the waves, which happened on Iwo Jima just a few years ago in 2023 . And experts expect the same thing to happen with this new land. "I imagine we'll see this new land wash away within a few months," Daniel Slayback, a scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center who has previously studied landforms created by volcanic eruptions, said in a statement . "But we'll have to wait and see."

It almost always ends up being totally fascinating, and only occasionally mildly traumatising. At a kid’s birthday party recently, I got chatting to one of the dads, who happens to be an ear, nose and throat consultant. I asked him if he used robotics for his surgeries. He said no, then proceeded to mime what he actually did instead. There followed a series of alarmingly enthusiastic slashing motions, like a scene from a horror movie, while in the background a group of 9-year-old girls sat quietly painting. Others tried a little pocket, with the same opening serving as entrance and exit. science.title: Astronomers discover the most distant and ancient supermassive black hole-powered quasar in the universe
science.description: null The Euclid space telescope has spotted the most distant and ancient quasar ever seen, a bright cosmic event powered by a supermassive black hole with 360 million times the mass of the sun. The supermassive black hole is seen as it was just 630 million years after the Big Bang. 40 million years further back in time than the previous record holder for the most ancient quasar. The discovery further deepens the mystery of how supermassive black holes grew so massive so soon into the history of the universe. That's because previously, scientists had theorized it should take 1 billion years of feeding and merging for black holes to reach supermassive status of millions or billions of times as massive as the sun. Quasars occur when supermassive black holes are surrounded by vast amounts of gas and dust on which they feed. The immense gravitational influence of the black hole causes this material, in the form of an accretion disk, to glow brightly and to blast out bright jets of plasma. That means quasars at the heart of galaxies in regions called active galactic nuclei (AGNs) like this one can often be brighter than the combined light of every star in the entire surrounding galaxy, but only briefly. The newly discovered quasar, designated J1504+6252 and nicknamed Dún Aonghasa, is in this brief phase of its existence. It was discovered among millions of objects in 18 months of data from Euclid. Euclid's initial observation of Dún Aonghasa was followed up by an array of ground-based and space-based telescopes, including the W.M. Keck Observatory, the Large Binocular Telescope Observatory, the Hubble Space Telescope , and ultimately the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). It was the JWST that determined the mass of this supermassive black hole. What is interesting about Dún Aonghasa is that it is unlike other supermassive black holes seen at a similar period of the early universe. That's because this black hole is feeding relatively slowly. That means if it engaged in rapid feeding to reach its massive size, that period of gorging on gas and dust has either ended or it has paused. The red dot at the center of this Euclid image is Dún Aonghasa (Image credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, Wolf et al. 2026) That is something that further complicates our picture of supermassive black hole growth. By staring back 13.1 billion years in time to see Dún Aonghasa, Euclid is also observing a crucial time in cosmic history when the first stars and galaxies were taking shape, and the clearing of cosmic gas was ending the dark ages of our universe by allowing light to travel freely. Euclid's primary mission is improving our understanding of dark energy , the mysterious force accelerating the expansion of the universe, and dark matter , the most mysterious "stuff" in the cosmos. Collectively, these aspects of the universe account for around 95% of its matter-energy budget and have come to be collectively referred to as the dark universe. Hence Euclid's nickname

NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin From the star of its namesake pie to a supporting player in countless side dishes, the pecan has earned a place on Thanksgiving tables across the United States. But before it becomes candied, chopped, or baked, it hangs from the branches of Carya illinoinensis —a species of hickory in the walnut family native to North America. Many U.S.-grown pecans come from orchards in Georgia, the state that has historically led the nation in production. One hotspot of pecan cultivation is in the southwest part of the state, around Albany, in Dougherty County. The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8 captured this image of the area and neighboring counties on October 23, 2026. That date falls within the pecan harvest season, which typically runs from October into December . In addition to pecans, other crops such as peanuts, cotton, and corn are also grown in the area. Landsat observations like these contribute to the Cropland Data Layer , an annual map of crop types across the contiguous United States produced by the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s National Agricultural Statistics Service . The 2025 map shows pecan groves clustered along the Flint River within the Coastal Plain . Pecan trees need abundant water, and they generally do well in the area’s well-drained sandy soils that sit above the Floridan aquifer system that growers can tap for irrigation. In the late 1800s, Georgia had less than 100 acres (40 hectares) of pecan orchards. Then, in the early 1900s, southwest Georgia’s Dougherty and Mitchell counties underwent a pecan boom when thousands of acres were planted and sold to investors . By the end of the 1950s, Georgia led the nation in pecan production, producing over 17 million pounds, according to 1959 agricultural census numbers . In recent decades, pecan production has grown in other states, such as New Mexico and Texas. Georgia faced challenges after Hurricane Michael damaged orchards in October 2018, and Hurricane Helene dealt another blow when it swept inland in September 2024. science.title: SpaceX launches secretive spy satellites from California for US Space Force (video)
science.description: null SpaceX launched another classified mission for the U.S. Space Force (USSF) today (Nov. 24), sending an unknown payload toward orbit from California. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Space Launch Complex-4E at TK11:08 a.m. ET (1508 GMT) , carrying the U.S. Space Force's USSF-266 mission. It was the fourth mission SpaceX has launched for the military branch this month. While details about the mission's payload weren't disclosed, it's the fifth space launch in support of U.S. national security in the last two weeks, and comes amid efforts by the Space Force to expand its communications and tracking capabilities. (Image credit: SpaceX) About two and a half minutes after liftoff, Falcon 9's first-stage booster separated from the rocket's upper stage, which continued toward low Earth orbit with the classified payload. The booster, meanwhile, began a descent toward SpaceX's Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific Ocean, where it touched down approximately eight and a half minutes after launch. Tuesday's launch marked the 29th flight for this Falcon 9 booster, B1081, which previously launched NASA 's Crew-7 astronaut mission to the International Space Station , the PACE and EarthCARE science satellites , two other classified Space Force launches (USSF-153 and USSF-481), and 16 Starlink missions. Previous classified Space Force launches have fueled speculation about the possible deployment of SpaceX's Starshield satellites, which are designed for national security applications. Starshield is an adapted spacecraft design developed from SpaceX's Starlink internet constellation that supports military operations with capabilities like Earth observation and secure communications. SpaceX has not confirmed whether USSF-266 is carrying Starshield spacecraft. USSF-266 follows three other classified Space Force missions launched by SpaceX from Vandenberg earlier this month: USSF-432 on Nov. 6, USSF-627 on Nov. 11 and USSF-317 on Nov. 20, as well as a National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) launch, NROL-136, on Nov. 22. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space
science.description: null On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere . After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets , the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched. Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space . (NASA and the U.S. military typically consider 50 miles the edge of space.) Mission control cut the flight short after about 30 seconds, because Aerobee started to yaw, and they wanted to keep it from going completely out of control. The first Aerobee sounding rocket launched on Nov. 24, 1947 under a project led by the U.S. Navy. (Image credit: U.S. Navy) Why it mattered Billed as the " most successful sounding rocket of the space age ," the initial Aerobee rocket was suborbital rocket designed to launch experment payload of up to 100 pounds (45 kilograms) to an altitude of 75 miles (121 kilometers) or so. "The Aerobee was designed to carry instruments aloft to collect data on the upper atmosphere and to place small animals in a weightless condition for physiological studies," the U.S. National Museum of the United States Air Force wrote in a mission overview . "It was launched by a solid-propellant booster engine of 18,000 pounds thrust that burned for only two and a half seconds." An Aerobee suborbital sounding rocket of the type designed to study Earth's atmosphere. (Image credit: NMMSH) While the first Aerobee rocket did not reach space , many more made successful launches in the decades that followed. Engineers made a steady stream of upgrades to the the Aerobee rocket, allowing to fly higher and launch heavier payloads into space. It was an Aerobee rocket that launched two Phillipine monkeys on a mission to study how the effects of rapid launch acceleration might affect their bodies, an experiment that was among the frst human physiology tests that paved the way for human spaceflight . More than 1,000 Aerobee rockets have launched since then, and the last one flew in January of 1985. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

science.title: Teams Lock in Mission Architecture for NASA’s SR-1 Freedom
science.description: 5 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) NASA’s Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, the first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth orbit, cruises past Mars in this artist’s concept, demonstrating nuclear electric propulsion in deep space. Credit: NASA/Jonathan North NASA completed a major review for Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom and locked in key elements of the spacecraft, which is targeted to launch in 2028 and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space for the first time. Experts from across the agency, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), and industry met at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland for a major SR-1 mission design review in October. Several key decisions were made, propelling the mission from an early concept toward a defined spacecraft design. “SR-1 marks a pivotal step in how we travel through the solar system,” said Steve Sinacore, SR-1 Freedom program director. “This mission will be the first freight run on the railroad of the solar system, and the decisions we’re making now are laying the tracks for every nuclear-powered spacecraft that follows.” Planned for launch in late 2028, SR-1 will use both nuclear and solar power to deliver SkyFall , a capsule carrying three next-generation helicopters, to Mars. Once deployed, the helicopters will study Martian geology and climate history, explore new terrain, and search for signs of subsurface ice. As NASA prepares for more ambitious exploration missions, future spacecraft and surface operations will require significantly more power than current systems can provide, particularly in environments where sunlight is limited or unavailable. SR-1 will demonstrate how fission power can enable long-duration missions, pave the way for reliable surface power systems to support NASA’s future Moon Base , and enable exploration deeper into the solar system. Key design decisions The SR-1 Freedom spacecraft design has evolved since NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman first introduced the concept in March at the agency’s Ignition event, where leadership shared plans to develop a fission-powered spacecraft in time for the next Mars launch window. One significant change is to use a shorter boom than the one shown in early illustrations. The boom separates the reactor from the spacecraft’s main body, known as the Power and Propulsion Element. The shorter boom will reduce weight, simplify assembly, and help streamline the spacecraft’s design. Planned for launch in late 2028, Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom will use both nuclear and solar power to deliver SkyFall to Mars. This infographic explains the components of the spacecraft. Credit: NASA/David Lam NASA and DOE experts also determined that improvements in shielding and spacecraft design will allow the reactor to operate closer to the rest of the spacecraft. This will simplify integration while maintaining the radiation protection needed for spacecraft electronics and the SkyFall payload.

science.title: 1st-ever detection of a dying star's 'final nuclear heartbeat' challenges what we know about our sun's eventual death
science.description: null As ubiquitous as the sun is to us today, our star is not eternal; one day, albeit in billions of years, it will die. While massive stars die in supernova explosions, the sun and stars of similar mass die quieter deaths. But that doesn't mean these stars completely go out with a whimper. New observations collected using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), the world's largest radio telescope comprised of 66 antennas in northern Chile, reveal that the sun's death throes may be different from what scientists had initially believed. NASA Jet Propulsion Lab (JPL) researcher Raghvendra Sahai, who led the investigation, explained the shape the ALMA observations took: "It's essentially a physical snapshot of an event that, until now, we've mostly inferred from theoretical models. We've caught, for the first time, a star's final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas." Sun-like stars "die" when they run out of hydrogen in their cores. This means that the fusion of hydrogen to helium ceases in the stellar core, and because this nuclear process is a star's main energy source, the star no longer has the outward push to support itself against the inward push of its own gravity. As the star's core collapses to create a stellar remnant called a white dwarf , the outer layers where hydrogen is still fusing to form helium swell out. This expansion leads to a relatively short-lived " red giant " phase. Eventually, these outer layers will cool and disperse, leaving the central white dwarf surrounded by a so-called "planetary nebula" shell of debris. During the red giant phase, as the stellar core is surrounded by shells of hydrogen and helium, these layers are occasionally rocked by flares in nuclear activity called thermal pulses. During these episodes, stellar material is flung into space. To better understand this phase in stellar evolution, the team focused ALMA on a star called IRAS 06530-0213, located around 12,000 light-years away in the constellation Monoceros. This revealed a giant ring of gas that appears to be a frozen fossil of the star's last thermonuclear flare-up. This thermonuclear fossil rings an hourglass-shaped planetary nebula in the act of forming. "Most of us think of stars as unchanging points of light, but this is a real-time snapshot of a star's death throes," Sahai said. "It's the brief, violent transition between a bloated red giant and a glowing planetary nebula, frozen mid-action." ALMA image of IRAS 06530-0213, revealing a giant ring of molecular gas surrounding a young, hourglass-shaped nebula. (Image credit: ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO); Sahai et al. science.title: Double asteroid solar eclipse caught on camera | Space photo of the day for Nov. 24, 2026
science.description: null (Image credit: ESA) A spacecraft far from Earth beamed home a rare sight: a solar eclipse caused by one asteroid casting its shadow on another. What is it? The image shows the Didymos double asteroid system , which consists of the larger Didymos and its moonlet, Dimorphos. In this image, Dimorphos' shadow can be seen on the surface of Didymos. The image was captured by the European Space Agency's (ESA's) Hera probe, which was sent to rendezvous with Didymos. Once there, Hera's job is to inspect the system to study the aftermath of NASA's historic DART mission (Double Asteroid Redirect Test), which slammed a kinetic impactor into Dimorphos in September 2022 in an attempt to alter its orbit and thus the trajectory of the entire two-asteroid system. Such missions, should they ever be needed in the future, could potentially redirect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. Why is it incredible? For one, this image is incredible given that it was beamed home by Hera while it approaches Didymos some 121 million miles (195 million kilometers) away from Earth. But more than that, this image reveals incredible details of the Didymos system. Scientists call Didymos a "rubble pile" asteroid , meaning it's a loose body made up of boulders, dust, gravel and other bits of the solar system held together by the asteroid's own gravity. In the image, many of these irregular boulders and rocks can be seen strewn across Didymos and its moonlet. Hera will reach the system on Nov. 25, and ESA will release the first full images from the mission.

science.title: China's Shenzhou-24 mission launches 1st international astronaut to Tiangong space station
science.description: null China has launed an international astronaut to its Tiangong space station today (Nov. 24) for the first time ever, marking a significant milestone for international participation in the Chinese space program. A Long March 2F rocket lifted off with the Shenzhou-24 crew from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China today at 7:18 p.m. EST (0018 GMT and 8:18 a.m. Beijing time on Nov. 25). You can watch the liftoff live here at Space.com, courtesy of China Central Television (CCTV). China rolls out the Long March 2F rocket for its Shenzhou-24 astronaut mission on Nov. 17, 2026. (Image credit: CCTV) Shenzhou-24 is China's 18th crewed spaceflight to date and its 12th astronaut mission to Tiangong , a three-module station that the nation finished assembling in low Earth orbit in late 2022. Those numbers may sound rather prosaic. But today's flight makes history, marking the first time that China has ever launched a foreign national to space. That trailblazer is Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a former pilot in Pakistan's armed forces who is the first person from his country ever to reach orbit. (Adventurer Namira Salim is the first Pakistani ever to fly to the final frontier, doing so on a Virgin Galactic suborbital mission in October 2023 .) China and Pakistan began paving Ali's path to Tiangong in February 2025 , with the signing of a spaceflight cooperation agreement in Islamabad. Pakistan then selected two astronaut candidates, who traveled to China for training. We didn't learn which Pakistani astronaut was picked for Shenzhou-24 until Monday night (Nov. 23), when China announced the mission's crew. This is not out of the ordinary, by the way; China generally doesn't reveal the identity of Shenzhou astronauts until the day before launch. This is in keeping with the nation's broader spaceflight ethos, which prizes keeping things close to the vest. Ali is flying as a payload specialist. The other Shenzhou-24 astronauts are commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer ​Wu Yi. Tang also flew on the Shenzhou-12 and Shenzhou-17 missions, which launched in June 2021 and October 2023, respectively. He will be the first person to visit Tiangong three times, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency. Shenzhou-24 will be the first spaceflight for Wu. Tang and Wu are expected to live aboard Tiangong for six months, the usual Shenzhou rotation. But Ali will stay in orbit for just a week or so, coming back down to Earth with Zhang Zhiyuan and Lai Ka-ying of the Shenzhou-23 mission, which launched on May 24 . According to the South China Morning Post, the third Shenzhou-23 crewmate, Zhu Yangzhu, will stay behind when Ali leaves, living aboard Tiangong until Shenzhou-24 comes home. Zhu will therefore become the first Chinese astronaut ever to spend a year in orbit, a milestone that will allow China to prep for long-duration missions to the moon and other deep-space locales.

science.title: Russia launches Progress 97 cargo ship to the International Space Station (video)
science.description: null Russia's latest freighter is on its way to the International Space Station. The robotic Progress 97 cargo craft launched atop a Soyuz rocket from the Russia-run Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan today (Nov. 24) at 5:17 a.m. EST (1013 GMT; 3:17 p.m. Baikonur time), carrying several tons of supplies for the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab. If all goes to plan, Progress 97 will arrive at the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday (Nov. 26), docking with its Poisk module. But the freighter won't stay at that particular locale for long. A Russian Soyuz rocket launches the uncrewed Progress 97 cargo ship to the International Space Station from Baikonur Cosmodrome, Kazakhstan on Nov. 24, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) The cosmonauts currently living on the ISS — Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and Sergey Teteryatnikov — will unload Progress 97 through Poisk. But the freighter will then hop over to a different port, according to journalist and space historian Anatoly Zak: the aft one of the PrK transfer tunnel, which leads to Russia's Zvezda service module. The PrK port is the best site for engine burns that boost the orbit of the ISS, a service that Progress freighters regularly provide. But Progress 97 cannot unload its cargo through that port because the PrK transfer tunnel has been sealed off, due to an ongoing air leak that was first documented in 2019. Progress-97 is therefore "the first cargo mission scheduled to unload its cargo and perform orbit corrections of the ISS at different docking ports," Zak wrote on the site he runs, RussianSpaceWeb.com. Progress 96 cargo spacecraft packed with science and supplies approaches the International Space Station for a docking on Sept. 19, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) The Progress 97 mission, which Russia calls Progress MS-36, was originally expected to launch this past August, according to Zak. But the liftoff was pushed back several times, most significantly by the collapse of the service platform at Baikonur's Site 31 in November 2025. It took Russia about three months to repair the platform, leading to a series of delays. Progress 97 will likely stay docked to the ISS for about six months, after which it will be loaded up with trash and sent home to burn up in Earth's atmosphere . Japan's HTV-X vehicle and Northrop Grumman's Cygnus spacecraft are similarly expendable. The only currently operational ISS cargo craft that's reusable is SpaceX's Dragon capsule, which makes parachute-aided ocean splashdowns at the end of its missions.

science.title: Watch November's full Beaver Moon live online today with supermoon livestream
science.description: null Editor's Note: The November full supermoon dazzled stargazers with a spectacular show overnight on Nov. 24. Check out our photo wrap article to see spectacular images of the "Beaver Moon" captured from around the world. November's full moon rises tonight (Nov. 24)! You can see live telescopic views of the "Beaver supermoon" courtesy of the Virtual Telescope Project (VTP). Today's stream features expert commentary from VTP founder Gianluca Masi, along with photos of previous full moons shining above historic landmarks in the heart of Rome. What makes the November full moon special? November's full moon is often called the Beaver Moon because it rises around the time the industrious animals are hard at work building dams and preparing for the winter months, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac .
